body.heading: An elevator for toys
paragraphs: Cranes, flagpoles and window-cleaners' platforms all share one humble hero: the pulley. It is just a wheel with a groove for a rope — but rig one over a frame and you can lift a load by pulling down, using your own body weight to help. Build this paper-cup elevator and feel the trick for yourself.

body.heading: Meet the parts
paragraphs: The wheel — a cotton reel or spool that spins freely; its groove keeps the string in line. The axle — the pencil or dowel the wheel turns on, held by the frame. The rope — string long enough to reach the floor. The load — a paper cup carrying toy bricks. And the effort — your hand, pulling down on the free end.

body.heading: You will need
paragraphs: A cotton reel or spool, a pencil or wooden dowel, string, a paper cup, two tall books or a cardboard frame, tape, a hole punch or a grown-up's help for the cup holes, and light loads — toy bricks, crayons or coins.

body.heading: How it works — step by step
paragraphs: Step 1 — Build the frame. Stand two tall books like towers (or tape a cardboard arch) and rest the pencil across the tops. Slide the spool onto the pencil so it spins freely.
Step 2 — Thread the string over the spool's groove. Tie one end to the paper cup — punch two small holes and tie through them so the cup hangs level.
Step 3 — Load the cup with two or three toy bricks. Now pull the free end of the string DOWN, slowly. The cup rises, smooth and straight.

Step 4 — Compare. Lift the same loaded cup straight up with your hand, no pulley. Same weight — but notice how the pulley let you pull down and lean your weight into it, instead of curling the load up with your fingers.

body.heading: The science bit
paragraphs: A single fixed pulley does not make the load lighter — it changes the direction of the force. Pulling down is easier than lifting up because you can add your body's weight to the pull, and your arms are stronger pulling down. Add a second pulley that moves with the load, and the rope shares the weight between two sections — that is when lifting truly gets lighter, and real cranes use whole teams of pulleys this way.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Where have you seen a pulley working in real life — a flagpole, a crane, a blind cord? What was it lifting?
2. Your model uses one fixed pulley. What do you predict would change if the pulley were tied to the CUP instead of the frame?

takeaway: A fixed pulley changes the direction of a pull — down instead of up — so your body weight helps you lift; extra pulleys share the load and make it lighter still.
materials: Cotton reel or spool (the pulley wheel)
Two tall books or a cardboard frame
Tape, and light loads: toy bricks, crayons or coins
supervision: A grown-up helps build the frame and punch holes, and checks the frame is steady before lifting begins.
safetyNotes: Light loads only — toy bricks and crayons. Never hang anything heavy, and never hang the pulley from a person or pet.
String can tangle and wrap — keep it away from necks, and put it away tidily when you finish; never leave string trailing on the floor.
Build on a table over a clear floor, so a falling cup lands on nothing and nobody.
screenFreeExtension: Elevator deliveries: set up a 'ground floor' and a 'top floor' (a chair or shelf a grown-up approves), and deliver soft toys up and down, counting how many trips your pulley makes in ten minutes.
